parts.problem_md:
Explore tragic events in Things Fall Apart.

You must consider the context of the novel in your answer.

**[40 marks]**
parts.solution_md:
### Model answer

Achebe builds Things Fall Apart as a tragedy in which a series of devastating events — some caused by Okonkwo's own flaws, some by colonial invasion — destroy both a great man and the world he belongs to.

The first great tragic event is the killing of Ikemefuna. The boy, taken from Mbaino, lives with Okonkwo for three years and comes to call him "father", yet when the Oracle decrees his death Okonkwo takes part in killing him. The elder Ezeudu warns, "That boy calls you father. Do not bear a hand in his death", but Okonkwo, "afraid of being thought weak", cuts him down. Achebe presents this as a tragic turning point caused by Okonkwo's deepest flaw — his terror of seeming weak — and in a culture that prized manliness, this fear drives him to a cruel act that haunts the rest of the novel. The boy's last cry, "My father, they have killed me", makes the betrayal painfully personal and shows how custom and fear together override love.

A second tragic event is Okonkwo's accidental killing of a clansman at Ezeudu's funeral, when his gun explodes. Because this is an accidental, "female" crime, Okonkwo is exiled to his motherland for seven years. Achebe uses this event to show how fate and chance, as well as character, shape tragedy: a single accident strips Okonkwo of the status he has spent his life building. The exile also removes him from Umuofia at the very moment the colonisers arrive, so that he returns to a world already changing beyond recognition.

The largest tragic event is the coming of the white missionaries and the colonial government. They build a church, win converts, and slowly undermine the customs that hold the community together. The threat of force is never far away: the news that "Abame has been wiped out" by the white man shows how easily the colonisers will answer resistance with massacre, and it warns Umuofia of the violence behind the new order. Achebe, writing back against colonial accounts of Africa, presents this not as simple progress but as a profound loss, dramatising a clash of cultures in which the Igbo world is dismissed and dismantled. Through the wise Obierika, Achebe sums up the tragedy: the white man "has put a knife on the things that held us together and we have fallen apart."

A further communal tragedy is the desecration of the clan's sacred world. When the zealous convert Enoch unmasks an egwugwu in public, the people feel that he has "killed an ancestral spirit", and in revenge the masked spirits burn down the "red-earth church". Achebe uses this clash of symbols to show the tragedy of a culture turning to violence to defend a sacred order that is already slipping away. The act gives the District Commissioner his excuse to imprison and humiliate the clan's leaders, so that an attempt to protect tradition only hastens its collapse.

Within this larger tragedy lies the personal tragedy of Okonkwo losing his son. Nwoye, always sensitive and drawn to gentler things, is moved by the new religion and converts to Christianity, abandoning his father. Achebe shows how the colonial intrusion divides families, and for Okonkwo, who longed for a strong son, Nwoye's conversion is a bitter blow that deepens his despair. The personal and the political tragedies feed each other, so that the breaking of the clan is also the breaking of a family.

The final tragic event is Okonkwo's death. After he kills a colonial messenger and the clan fails to rise with him, Okonkwo, seeing that his world will not fight, hangs himself. Achebe makes this doubly tragic: suicide is an abomination in Igbo belief, so the great man cannot even be buried by his own people. Obierika's furious words to the District Commissioner — "That man was one of the greatest men in Umuofia. You drove him to kill himself" — capture the waste of it. Achebe then sharpens the tragedy with bitter irony, as the Commissioner imagines reducing Okonkwo's whole life to a single paragraph in his book on pacifying the tribes.

Through Ikemefuna's death, Okonkwo's exile, the colonial invasion, Nwoye's conversion and Okonkwo's suicide, Achebe builds a layered tragedy. He shows a proud man destroyed partly by his own flaws and partly by the destruction of his entire culture, so that the fall of one man becomes the fall of a whole world.

parts.problem_md:
“Okonkwo was ruled by one passion – to hate everything that his father Unoka had loved. One of those things was gentleness and another was idleness.”

Discuss the character of Unoka and his effect on others in the novel.

You must consider the context of the novel in your answer.

**[40 marks]**
parts.solution_md:
### Model answer

Achebe presents Unoka as a gentle, music-loving failure whose weakness shames his son Okonkwo so deeply that the whole of Okonkwo's life — and much of the tragedy — grows from his determination not to be like his father.

Unoka is presented as the opposite of everything his society admires. He is "lazy and improvident", a debtor who owes every neighbour, and he dies without taking a single title. Achebe shows him happiest "on his flute", loving music, good food and good company. In a culture that measured a man by hard work, yam harvests and titles, Unoka is a failure — yet Achebe gives him a warmth and love of beauty that the harsh society around him cannot value, quietly inviting the reader to see worth where Umuofia sees none.

Unoka's failure is most shameful in a society built on war and courage. Achebe tells us plainly that Unoka "was in fact a coward and could not bear the sight of blood", turning instead to music whenever talk of war arose. In a warrior culture where bravery wins a man his place, this cowardice fixes Unoka's disgrace, and Achebe uses it to explain Okonkwo directly: the son who later becomes a fearless fighter and head-taker is reacting against exactly this weakness. The contrast shows how a father's shame can drive a child to the opposite, and equally dangerous, extreme.

Unoka's deepest effect is the shame he plants in Okonkwo. Achebe tells us Okonkwo "was ruled by one passion—to hate everything that his father Unoka had loved", including "gentleness" and "idleness". Okonkwo's whole personality is built in reaction against his father, so that he becomes harsh, driven and violent precisely because Unoka was soft and weak. Achebe uses this to show how a parent's failure can shape a child as powerfully as any success, twisting Okonkwo into the opposite of the man who raised him.

Unoka is also the source of Okonkwo's defining fear. Achebe writes that Okonkwo's life was "dominated by fear, the fear of failure and of weakness" — the fear of becoming his father. This fear drives Okonkwo's greatest mistakes, including his part in Ikemefuna's death, when he acts because he is "afraid of being thought weak". Through Unoka, Achebe shows that the roots of the tragedy lie in Okonkwo's terror of resembling the gentle man he despised.

Unoka also lets Achebe explore the values of Igbo society. The community judges Unoka harshly, and a worthless, titleless man is mocked as "agbala" — a word that also means "woman" — which shows how closely failure and weakness were tied to femininity. Achebe uses Unoka to question this rigid idea of masculinity: the gentle, artistic father is despised, while the violent, "successful" son is admired, even though it is the son's harshness that finally destroys him.

Even Unoka's death deepens his effect on the novel. Because he "died of the swelling which was an abomination to the earth goddess", he "had no grave" and "was carried to the Evil Forest and left there to die", denied the dignified burial Umuofia gives its respected men. Achebe makes this shameful end echo at the very close of the book, when Okonkwo's suicide turns his own body into an abomination his kinsmen may not touch. Father and son, so opposite in life, are finally joined by a disgraced death, and it is a bitter irony that the man who built his whole identity on being everything Unoka was not should end by sharing his father's fate exactly. Through this grim parallel Achebe suggests that Okonkwo never truly escaped the father he spent his life running from.

Although Unoka is a failure by his society's standards, Achebe treats him with quiet sympathy. His love of music and the seasons, and his easy contentment, hint at a fuller, gentler way of being human than Okonkwo's grim drive allows. Achebe even gives Unoka a kind of homely wisdom about life's ups and downs. By the end, the reader may feel that Okonkwo's contempt for his father costs him dearly, since it is exactly the gentleness Unoka loved that Okonkwo most lacks, and most needs.

Achebe presents Unoka as a gentle failure whose shadow falls across the whole novel. His effect on Okonkwo — the shame, the fear, the hatred of weakness — shapes the proud, harsh man whose flaws drive the tragedy, making Unoka far more important than his small role suggests.

parts.problem_md:
How is Nwoye presented in the novel?

You must consider the context of the novel in your answer.

**[40 marks]**
parts.solution_md:
### Model answer

Achebe presents Nwoye as a sensitive boy crushed by his father's harshness, whose eventual conversion to Christianity dramatises both Okonkwo's personal tragedy and the wider breaking apart of Igbo society.

Nwoye is presented from the start as gentle and sensitive, unlike his father. As a boy he is drawn to his mother's folk tales rather than to violent stories of war, and Achebe shows him "developing into a sad-faced youth" under his father's "constant nagging and beating". In a society that prized manliness and strength, Nwoye's softness marks him out, and Achebe uses him to show the human cost of Okonkwo's rigid idea of what a man should be.

From boyhood Achebe sets Nwoye's nature against his father's through the stories each prefers. Okonkwo tells "masculine stories of violence and bloodshed", but Nwoye secretly still loves his mother's gentler tales of "the tortoise and his wily ways" and of the birds. Achebe shows Nwoye learning to feign enthusiasm for his father's war stories to please him, so that the boy hides his true, tender nature from very early on. This long habit of suppressing himself roots the later conversion in a lifetime of quiet unhappiness rather than in sudden rebellion. Even as a small boy, then, Nwoye is quietly at odds with the world his father rules.

Nwoye is significant as the source of Okonkwo's deep disappointment. Okonkwo, terrified of weakness, sees his own father's softness in his son and despairs of him, even wishing his fierce daughter Ezinma had been a boy instead. Achebe uses this to show how Okonkwo's fear poisons even his love for his children. The harder Okonkwo pushes and beats, the further Nwoye drifts, so that father and son grow steadily and tragically apart.

The turning point for Nwoye is the killing of Ikemefuna, whom he had loved like an elder brother. When Ikemefuna is killed — with Okonkwo's own hand — something breaks in Nwoye. Achebe presents this as the moment Nwoye begins to question the customs of his people, since a beloved boy who called Okonkwo "father" could be killed in the name of tradition. The same quiet horror had already stirred in him at the practice of leaving twins to die in the forest, and Achebe links these two memories to show a gentle conscience slowly turning against the harsher demands of custom.

Nwoye's conversion to Christianity is his most significant act. What draws him is not doctrine but feeling: Achebe writes that it was "the poetry of the new religion" that captivated him, and that as the missionaries' hymn was sung he "felt a relief within". The song about brothers sitting in darkness seems to answer the very questions that had troubled him, the killing of Ikemefuna and the abandoning of twins, so that the new faith offers comfort where the old world offered only fear. Through this, Achebe dramatises how colonialism won the hearts of those the old society had failed or frightened, drawing them gently away from their own people.

The break between father and son becomes final after Nwoye joins the missionaries. When Okonkwo hears of it he half-strangles the boy, and Nwoye leaves his father's compound for good. Achebe then shows Okonkwo brooding by his fire, the "Roaring Flame" wondering "how then could he have begotten a son like Nwoye, degenerate and effeminate". The metaphor that follows — "Living fire begets cold, impotent ash" — captures his despair exactly: all his fierce energy has produced only a son he sees as lifeless and weak. Achebe makes Nwoye the proof that Okonkwo's harsh manliness cannot reproduce itself, and that his line, as he sees it, has failed.

Nwoye's importance is both personal and historical. For Okonkwo, his son's conversion is a devastating blow, proof that his line and his values will not continue. For the novel as a whole, Nwoye represents the younger generation drawn away from tradition, showing how the community falls apart from within as well as from outside. Achebe makes Nwoye a quiet but crucial figure: through him we see both a father's failure and a culture's loss at the same moment.

Achebe presents Nwoye as a gentle boy broken by his father's harshness and won over by a new faith. Through his sensitivity, his horror at Ikemefuna's death and his conversion, Nwoye embodies both Okonkwo's personal tragedy and the wider unravelling of Igbo society.

parts.problem_md:
Explore the theme of respect in Things Fall Apart.

You must consider the context of the novel in your answer.

**[40 marks]**
parts.solution_md:
### Model answer

Achebe presents respect as the value that rules Igbo society, showing how the community's deep respect for achievement, age and custom shapes Okonkwo's life, and how the loss of that respect finally destroys him.

In Umuofia, respect is earned through achievement. Okonkwo wins fame young by throwing the great wrestler "Amalinze the Cat", becoming "one of the greatest men of his time". Achebe shows a society in which "achievement was revered" above all, where a man rises through hard work, yam harvests, titles and bravery in war. Okonkwo's hunger for this respect drives his whole life, making him work furiously to escape the shame of his idle father.

Respect in this society is tightly bound to manliness. A man with no title is mocked as "agbala", a word that also means "woman", so that weakness and femininity are despised. Achebe uses this to show how the community's idea of respect pressures men to be hard and even violent. Okonkwo so fears losing respect that he beats his wives and takes part in Ikemefuna's death rather than appear weak, showing how the demand for respect can drive men to cruelty.

Yet respect is not only for achievement; it is also owed to age and to those who guide the clan. Achebe is careful to note that "age was respected" even as achievement was revered, so that elders like Ezeudu carry real authority. When Ezeudu warns Okonkwo, "Do not bear a hand" in Ikemefuna's death, his word should command respect, and Okonkwo's decision to ignore it shows how his fear of seeming weak overrides the proper respect owed to an elder. Achebe uses this to suggest that Okonkwo's tragedy partly springs from respecting the wrong things, valuing his own reputation above the wisdom of those older than him.

Achebe also shows respect for tradition, the gods and the elders. The community respects the Oracle, the egwugwu who embody the ancestors, and customs like the sacred Week of Peace; even Okonkwo is punished when he breaks the peace by beating his wife. Through the wise Obierika, "a man who thought about things", Achebe shows that this respect for custom is not blind: thoughtful members of the community can question some practices even while they honour the rest.

Respect also runs through the small rituals of daily life, above all the breaking of the kola nut. When a guest arrives, the host offers kola with the words "He who brings kola brings life", and the careful etiquette of who breaks it and how it is shared marks the mutual respect that binds neighbours together. Achebe dwells on these courtesies to show that respect in Umuofia is not only about titles and bravery but about a shared code of manners, observed patiently in even the smallest meeting. By rooting respect in everyday custom, he makes its later collapse feel like the loss of a whole way of living rather than of one man's standing — the very thing Obierika mourns when he says the white man has broken the things "that held us together".

The arrival of the colonisers is a crisis of respect. The missionaries and the District Commissioner show no respect for Igbo customs, gods or leaders, treating them as primitive. Achebe, writing back against such colonial attitudes, dramatises the wound this causes through Obierika's lament that the white man "has put a knife on the things that held us together". When the community can no longer command respect, it begins to fall apart, and men like Okonkwo lose the world that gave their lives meaning.

Okonkwo's tragedy is the loss of the respect he lived for. After his exile and the colonial takeover, his violent stand against the messengers wins him no followers, and in despair he takes his own life. Because suicide is an abomination, he is denied an honourable burial — the ultimate loss of respect. Obierika's furious words, "That man was one of the greatest men in Umuofia. You drove him to kill himself", show how a society's collapse can strip even its greatest man of the respect he earned.

Achebe presents respect as the foundation of Igbo society and the force that both makes and destroys Okonkwo. His drive for respect builds him up, his fear of losing it leads him into cruelty, and the colonial destruction of his world's respect finally brings him down.

parts.problem_md:
How is Obierika presented in the novel?

You must consider the context of the novel in your answer.

**[40 marks]**
parts.solution_md:
### Model answer

Achebe presents Obierika as Okonkwo's wise, thoughtful friend, using him as a calm, questioning voice that lets the reader understand both the strengths of Igbo society and the tragedy of its destruction.

Obierika is introduced as a contrast to Okonkwo. Achebe describes him simply as "a man who thought about things", whereas Okonkwo acts on instinct and pride. Obierika is loyal and generous — he looks after Okonkwo's yams and property during the seven years of his exile — but he also reflects on the meaning of events rather than just reacting to them. Achebe uses this thoughtful nature to give the novel a steady voice of reason amid Okonkwo's violence and haste.

Obierika's mixture of loyalty and quiet doubt is clearest when Okonkwo is exiled. After Okonkwo's gun goes off by accident at Ezeudu's funeral and kills a boy, custom demands that the clan burn his houses and drive him out, and Obierika dutifully takes part. Yet that same evening, sitting alone, he asks himself "Why should a man suffer so grievously for an offense he had committed inadvertently?" Achebe uses this private question to show a man who obeys his society's laws while still feeling their harshness, and who keeps faith with his friend by carefully looking after his yams through all seven years of exile. His loyalty is active, not sentimental, and it sits side by side with a conscience that custom cannot fully satisfy.

Obierika is significant because he gently questions traditions that Okonkwo never doubts. After the killing of Ikemefuna, Obierika quietly criticises Okonkwo's part in it, and he wonders about customs such as the throwing away of twins. Achebe uses Obierika to show that Igbo society is not simple or unthinking: it contains people fully capable of reflection and doubt. This directly counters the colonial idea of "primitive" tribes, since the novel's wisest voice belongs to an Igbo man.

Achebe shows the depth of this questioning most clearly in Obierika's private grief. Sitting alone after Okonkwo's exile, Obierika remembers his own "twin children, whom he had thrown away", and asks himself, "What crime had they committed?" Through this quiet, inward doubt, Achebe presents a man who honours custom yet cannot silence his own conscience, finding "no answer" to why the gods demand such suffering. By giving the clan's most respected thinker these troubling questions, Achebe shows that Igbo culture contained its own capacity for moral reflection long before the missionaries arrived.

Obierika often serves as the reader's window into events. Because he thinks and asks questions, his conversations explain customs and reactions that might otherwise seem strange to an outside reader. Achebe uses him to bridge the gap between the Igbo world and the audience, presenting that world from the inside with sympathy and intelligence. Through Obierika, the novel argues for the value and complexity of the very culture the colonisers dismiss.

Achebe also uses Obierika to carry news that shapes the novel's structure. It is Obierika who travels to Mbanta to visit Okonkwo in exile and brings word of the white men — first the wiping out of the neighbouring village of Abame, then the growing power of the church and the colonial court in Umuofia. By making the thoughtful Obierika the messenger, Achebe lets each new threat arrive already weighed and understood, so the reader feels the slow, dawning dread of a world quietly being taken apart rather than a sudden invasion.

As the colonisers take hold, Obierika becomes the voice that names the tragedy. It is he who delivers the novel's central image: the white man "has put a knife on the things that held us together and we have fallen apart". Achebe gives this line to Obierika rather than Okonkwo because Obierika understands what is happening, while Okonkwo can only rage and long to fight. This makes Obierika the character who grasps the meaning of the disaster most clearly.

Obierika's importance peaks at the end. Gazing at his friend's "dangling body", he turns "ferociously" on the District Commissioner: "That man was one of the greatest men in Umuofia. You drove him to kill himself." Achebe gives Obierika this furious dignity to speak for the whole community's grief and anger, and to expose the cruelty of the colonisers. In a novel about a man who could never express his feelings, it is fitting that Obierika finally speaks the truth Okonkwo never could.

Achebe presents Obierika as the thoughtful conscience of the novel: a loyal friend who questions custom, explains his world to the reader, and finally names the tragedy. Through him, Achebe defends the richness of Igbo culture and voices the grief of its destruction.

parts.problem_md:
In what ways are Igbo (Ibo in the novel) traditions important in Things Fall Apart?

You must consider the context of the novel in your answer.

**[40 marks]**
parts.solution_md:
### Model answer

Achebe makes Igbo traditions central to the novel, presenting a rich, ordered culture whose customs give life meaning — and whose destruction by colonialism is the heart of the tragedy.

From the opening, Achebe presents Igbo traditions as the foundation of a structured, meaningful world. Life revolves around the yam harvest, wrestling contests, title-taking and the rhythm of the seasons, and a man earns his place through custom and achievement. Achebe describes this world in loving, careful detail so that the reader sees it as ordered and dignified, deliberately countering colonial images of Africa as savage or chaotic. The traditions are not background; they are the very structure of the characters' lives.

Religious tradition shapes every part of life. The community honours the Oracle, "Agbala" of the Hills and Caves, the egwugwu who embody the ancestors, and customs such as the sacred Week of Peace. Achebe shows the real power of these beliefs when Okonkwo is punished for breaking the peace by beating his wife. Through such customs, Achebe presents a society with its own deep spiritual order, as real and as demanding as any organised religion the colonisers might recognise.

Tradition also provides Umuofia with its own system of justice and government. When a dispute arises between Uzowulu and his wife's family, it is settled not by violence but by the egwugwu — masked figures embodying the ancestors — who hear the evidence in a public ceremony. Their leader, Evil Forest, greets each man with the ritual "Uzowulu's body, I salute you", and only after "We have heard both sides of the case" delivers a measured judgement. Achebe presents this as a dignified, ordered legal process, every bit as serious as a European court. By showing the clan governing itself so carefully, he counters the colonial assumption that the Igbo had no real institutions, and makes the later imposition of the District Commissioner's court feel not like the arrival of justice but the destruction of a justice that already existed. Here, as so often, Achebe lets the patient detail of custom do the arguing for him.

Tradition is also kept alive through the spoken word. Achebe tells us that "the art of conversation is regarded very highly" among the Igbo, and that "proverbs are the palmoil with which words are eaten", so that wisdom passes from old to young in everyday speech. Folk tales matter just as much: the gentle stories Nwoye loves to hear from his mother carry the values of the community. Through this oral tradition, Achebe shows that Igbo culture has its own rich learning, handed down by voice rather than by the written word the colonisers bring — a quiet rebuke to the idea that a society without books has no civilisation.

Achebe does not idealise tradition; he shows its harsher side too. Twins are thrown away as an "abomination", the outcast osu are shunned, and the Oracle can demand a death, as it does with Ikemefuna. Achebe presents these customs honestly, allowing thoughtful characters like Obierika and the sensitive Nwoye to feel troubled by them. This balance makes the portrait of Igbo tradition convincing rather than sentimental, and it helps explain why some, like Nwoye, are later drawn towards the new religion.

Igbo traditions are important because they give the characters their very identity. A man's worth, a family's honour and the community's unity all rest on shared custom. Achebe shows how deeply these traditions bind people together, so that to lose them is to lose oneself. This is why the colonial attack on custom is so devastating: it does not just change a few rules, it dissolves the things that make people who they are.

The tragedy of the novel is the breaking of these traditions by colonialism. The missionaries win converts, the colonial court overrules custom, and the unity of the clan dissolves. Achebe voices the loss through Obierika: the white man "has put a knife on the things that held us together and we have fallen apart". When Okonkwo's suicide leaves him unable to be buried according to his own people's customs, Achebe shows how completely the traditional world has been undone.

Achebe makes Igbo traditions the living heart of the novel — an ordered, spiritual, sometimes harsh world that gives the characters meaning and identity. Their destruction by colonialism is the central tragedy, and the loss of that shared custom is what truly makes things fall apart.

parts.problem_md:
How is Okonkwo presented in Things Fall Apart?

You must consider the context of the novel in your answer.

**[40 marks]**
parts.solution_md:
### Model answer

Achebe presents Okonkwo as a tragic hero: a great and powerful man whose strength is also his flaw, so that the very qualities that make him admired finally destroy him.

Okonkwo is first presented as a self-made great man. Famous throughout "the nine villages" for throwing the wrestler "Amalinze the Cat", he rises through hard work and bravery to become "one of the greatest men of his time". Achebe shows him achieving everything his society values — barns of yams, titles, a large compound — entirely through his own effort. In a culture that respected achievement above age, Okonkwo is a hero who has earned his place from nothing.

Yet Achebe shows that Okonkwo's strength comes from fear. His whole life is "dominated by fear, the fear of failure and of weakness" — above all the fear of resembling his gentle, idle father, Unoka. Achebe presents this fear as the engine of Okonkwo's success but also the seed of his downfall, since it makes him unable to show tenderness and quick to use violence. His deepest flaw is that he equates manliness with hardness, and weakness with shame.

This flaw shapes Okonkwo's life at home as well as in the village. Achebe tells us he "ruled his household with a heavy hand", beating his wives and children, because for him "to show affection was a sign of weakness". The cost of this is clearest with his daughter Ezinma, whom he loves but cannot openly cherish; he can only wish, "She should have been a boy". Achebe uses this suppressed tenderness to deepen the tragedy, showing a man whose rigid idea of manliness starves even his own warmest feelings, so that his harshness wounds those he most cares for.

This flaw also drives Okonkwo's worst act. Warned by Ezeudu, "Do not bear a hand" in Ikemefuna's death, Okonkwo nonetheless kills the boy who had called him "father" because he is "afraid of being thought weak". Achebe presents this as the tragic flaw made visible: Okonkwo's terror of weakness overrides love, custom and wisdom alike. The act haunts him and marks the true beginning of his decline.

Okonkwo's tragedy deepens through events partly beyond his control. His accidental killing of a clansman sends him into seven years of exile, and he returns to find the colonisers established and his own son converted. Achebe shows Okonkwo unable to adapt to this changed world: where the thoughtful Obierika understands what is happening, Okonkwo can only long to fight. His rigid strength, once his greatest asset, leaves him stranded in a world that no longer rewards it.

Okonkwo's flaw shows again in how he endures his exile. Sent to live in his motherland, Mbanta, he treats the seven years as a humiliating interruption rather than a refuge, and his uncle Uchendu has to rebuke him for his ingratitude. Uchendu reminds him that one of the commonest names the Igbo give their children is "Nneka", meaning "Mother is Supreme" — that a man should find comfort in his motherland when life beats him down. Achebe uses this lesson to expose the limits of Okonkwo's hard, masculine code: he cannot accept the gentler, feminine wisdom Uchendu offers, and spends his exile longing only to return and reassert himself. His inability to bend, even when his own culture offers him solace, prepares the reader for his final refusal to adapt to the changed world he comes home to, and is one more sign that his greatest enemy is his own inflexibility.

Okonkwo's end completes the tragedy. When he kills a colonial messenger and the clan does not rise with him, he sees that his world will not fight, and he hangs himself. Achebe makes this doubly bitter: suicide is an abomination, so the great man is to be "buried like a dog", and the District Commissioner coldly imagines reducing his life to a paragraph in a book. Through Obierika's furious grief — "You drove him to kill himself" — Achebe shows the waste of a great man destroyed by his own inflexibility and by the collapse of his culture.

Achebe presents Okonkwo as a true tragic hero, great and admired yet undone by the fear and rigidity at the heart of his strength. His personal fall mirrors the fall of his whole society, so that one man's tragedy becomes the tragedy of a world.
